title: What Is Radio?

signals.name: FM broadcast
signals.blurb: An FM broadcast example at 98.100 MHz.

signals.name: 2-meter amateur
signals.blurb: 146.520 MHz is in the amateur 2-meter region.

signals.name: 70-centimeter amateur
signals.blurb: 446.000 MHz is in the amateur 70-centimeter region.

blocks.body: Several signals are already around this receiver. Tuning changes only the frequency this receiver is listening to.

config.prompt: If you move your receiver away from 146.520 MHz, what happens to the 146.520 MHz signal?
choices: The 146.520 MHz signal stays put. This receiver just stops listening there.
The transmitter follows the dial and starts sending on the new frequency.
The signal switches off because this receiver is no longer listening.
The signal's frequency becomes whatever this receiver's display shows.
choiceNotes: The signal stays at 146.520 MHz. You only changed which frequency this receiver is listening to.
The tuning control does not retune a transmitter or start it transmitting.
A signal can still be there when this receiver is listening somewhere else.
The display shows this receiver's frequency. It does not rewrite the other signals.

blocks.prompt: This simulation is a teaching model of a repeating wave, not a radio wave moving through space.

config.prompt: Compared with 1 cycle in this window, 8 cycles means:
choices: The wave is repeating more slowly.
More cycles fit in the same interval, so the frequency is higher.
The window got longer, so the count does not change the rate.
Each cycle lasts one second no matter how many you see.
choiceNotes: Fewer cycles in the same window would be the slower rate.
Frequency is how many cycles happen each second. More cycles in the same interval is a higher frequency. 1 cycle per second is 1 hertz.
The window stayed the same. What changed is how many cycles fit inside it.
A cycle is one repeat. How many fit into one second is the frequency in hertz.

config.prompt: If frequency increases, what do you predict will happen to wavelength?
choices: Wavelength gets shorter.
Wavelength gets longer, because a bigger frequency is a bigger wave.
Wavelength stays the same. Frequency and wavelength are separate.
Wavelength becomes the same number as the frequency.
choiceNotes: Test that prediction on the wave model. Higher frequency packs the repeats closer together.
A bigger frequency number does not mean a longer wave. Try the higher-frequency button and compare the spacing.
They are tied together. Change the frequency and watch the spacing between repeats.
The frequency number is not the wavelength. Wavelength is the distance of one repeat.

calculations.prompt: About how many meters is the wavelength at 146 MHz? Use 300 ÷ frequency in MHz.
About how many meters is the wavelength at 446 MHz? Use 300 ÷ frequency in MHz.

blocks.prompt: You have a receiver and want to listen to the weather channel at 162.550 MHz. Use the tuning control, then answer the questions in order.

config.meaningPrompt: The 162.550 in 162.550 MHz is telling you:
meaningChoices: How many miles the broadcast travels.
The frequency, counted in millions of hertz.
Which volume step the receiver should use.
meaningNotes: Miles would be a distance. MHz is a frequency unit.
MHz means megahertz: how many millions of cycles each second.
Megahertz measures frequency. Wavelength for this signal is a fraction of a few meters, not 162.550 MHz.
The number is the frequency to tune, not a volume setting.
config.comparePrompt: Which signal has the shorter wavelength?
compareChoices: They match, because both are radio frequencies.
Whichever one this receiver is tuned to.
compareNotes: 162.550 MHz is the lower frequency here, so its wavelength is longer.
446.000 MHz is the higher frequency, so each cycle takes less distance.
Tuning this receiver does not change either signal's wavelength.
config.awayPrompt: You tune this receiver from 162.550 MHz to 146.520 MHz. What happens?
awayChoices: The weather broadcast moves to 146.520 MHz with the dial.
The weather broadcast stays at 162.550 MHz. This receiver is now listening at 146.520 MHz.
The weather broadcast turns off until you tune back.
Both signals change frequency by the same amount.
awayNotes: The dial does not move the weather broadcast.
You changed the receiver's selected frequency. The weather signal is still at 162.550 MHz.
Stopping listening does not stop the broadcast.
The receiver moved. The signals stayed on their own frequencies.

blocks.prompt: Say what changed, and what did not, without looking up the earlier answers.

checks.prompt: You are listening to a station on 146.520 MHz and turn your receiver to 146.550 MHz. What changed?
choices: The station started transmitting on 146.550 MHz.
This receiver's listening frequency changed to 146.550 MHz.
The station's wavelength became 146.550 meters.
The signal strength of every station changed.
choiceNotes: Turning this receiver does not make the station change frequency or start transmitting.
You changed the frequency this receiver is listening to.
146.550 MHz is a frequency, not a wavelength in meters.
Moving the dial selects a frequency. It does not raise or lower every signal.

checks.prompt: In that same change, what did not change?
choices: The station is still at 146.520 MHz.
This receiver is still listening at 146.520 MHz.
The station turned its carrier off.
The station's frequency became 146.550 MHz too.
choiceNotes: The original signal is still at 146.520 MHz.
The receiver display would now read 146.550 MHz.
Looking away does not switch the station off.
Only this receiver's setting changed.

checks.prompt: Why is the wavelength near 446 MHz shorter than the wavelength near 146 MHz?
choices: Because 446 is a larger frequency, and higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
Because 446 MHz is closer to the receiver, so the wave shrinks.
Because UHF waves are assigned a fixed length of 70 centimeters no matter the frequency.
Because dividing 300 by a larger number makes a longer wavelength.
choiceNotes: Wavelength in meters is about 300 divided by the frequency in MHz. A larger frequency gives a smaller result.
Distance from the receiver is not what sets the wavelength.
The band name comes from the wavelength. The wavelength still follows the frequency.
Dividing 300 by a larger number gives a shorter wavelength, not a longer one.

questions.stem: You are receiving a signal on 146.520 MHz and turn the receiver to 146.550 MHz. Which statement is correct?
choices: The transmitter moved to 146.550 MHz because the receiver did.
The signal and the receiver both shifted up by 30 kHz.
The receiver is now listening at 146.550 MHz. The 146.520 MHz signal is still there.
The 146.520 MHz signal stopped because you stopped listening to it.
choiceNotes: You changed the receiver's selected frequency. The transmitter did not follow the dial.
Only the receiver moved. The original signal is still at 146.520 MHz.
You changed the receiver's selected frequency. The original signal is still at 146.520 MHz.
You changed the receiver's selected frequency. The original signal is still at 146.520 MHz.

choices: How far the station is, in millions of meters.
How many millions of cycles the wave completes each second.
A signal-strength reading of 146.
The wavelength, written in megahertz.
choiceNotes: Distance would be meters or miles. Megahertz is a frequency unit.
146.520 MHz means 146.520 million cycles each second.
Signal strength in this lab is a small scale, not the frequency readout.
Megahertz names the frequency. Wavelength is the distance of one cycle, in meters.
That kept the megahertz digits. 1 MHz = 1,000 kHz, so multiply by 1,000.
That slipped a decimal place. 162.550 × 1,000 = 162,550.
That used the hertz factor. Kilohertz is 1,000 hertz, and 1 MHz is 1,000 kHz, so the kilohertz number is 162,550.

questions.stem: A signal near 146 MHz has a wavelength of about 2 meters. You compare it with a signal near 446 MHz. What is true of the wavelength?
choices: It gets longer, because 446 is a bigger number than 146.
It stays about 300 meters, because the formula always starts from 300.
It gets shorter, to under 1 meter.
It becomes 446 meters, because the frequency number is the wavelength.
choiceNotes: A bigger frequency gives a shorter wavelength. Use 300 ÷ frequency in MHz.
300 is divided by the frequency in MHz. It is not the wavelength by itself.
446 MHz is higher, so the wavelength is shorter: about 300 ÷ 446, under 1 meter.
That copied the frequency. Wavelength in meters is about 300 ÷ 446.

questions.stem: You are listening to weather radio at 162.550 MHz, then tune the receiver to 146.520 MHz. What is true?
choices: The weather broadcast is still at 162.550 MHz. This receiver is now listening at 146.520 MHz.
The weather broadcast moved to 146.520 MHz with the dial.
The weather broadcast's wavelength became about 2 meters because you tuned away.
The receiver is still listening at 162.550 MHz until the weather station changes frequency.
choiceNotes: You changed the receiver's selected frequency. The weather signal is still at 162.550 MHz.
The dial does not move the weather broadcast. It is still at 162.550 MHz.
Tuning away does not change the weather signal's wavelength. About 2 meters belongs near 146 MHz.
The receiver is now listening at 146.520 MHz. The weather broadcast did not have to change.

blocks.prompt: Finish both checklist items. The field task is recorded only when both are done. Center the receiver so the readout shows 162.550 MHz. Then answer the question about that weather signal.

config.prompt: You set this receiver to 162.550 MHz, then tune it to 146.520 MHz. What is true of the weather signal?
choices: It stays at 162.550 MHz. This receiver is now listening at 146.520 MHz.
It moves to 146.520 MHz because you turned the tuning control.
It turns off until the readout comes back to 162.550 MHz.
Its wavelength changes to about 2 meters.
choiceNotes: You changed the receiver's selected frequency. The weather signal is still at 162.550 MHz.
The tuning control does not move the weather signal. It is still at 162.550 MHz.
The weather signal does not depend on this receiver staying tuned to it.
Tuning the receiver does not change the weather signal's wavelength.
